record.title: U.S. Treasury proposes prohibiting covered outbound investment in development of defined AI systems for countries of concern
record.summary: The U.S. Treasury published a proposed outbound-investment rule on Oct 26, 2026. It would implement the COINS Act framework and classify development of a defined “super intelligence system” as prohibited, rather than notifiable, technology in covered U.S.-person transactions involving countries of concern. The proposed definition includes generative systems and certain software, hardware, applications, tools or utilities operating with them. Treasury estimates annual direct compliance costs of $2.772–$5.86 million and about 20,000 person-hours, based on an estimated 200 potentially covered transactions; for its notification-cost estimate, it assumes all 200 are notifiable. These are ex ante regulatory estimates, not observed costs. Separately, Treasury estimates $4–$5 million in government IT development costs, $2–$3 million in annual system maintenance, and under $1 million in FY2027 personnel costs; it has no specific estimates for future outreach and enforcement. The proposal is open for comment through Dec 7, 2026, not current law; final scope and realized effects remain unknown.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: On Oct 26, 2026, the U.S. Treasury published a proposed rule to implement the COINS Act outbound-investment framework; written comments are due Dec 7, 2026. The proposal is not a final rule.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The proposed rule would classify development of a defined “super intelligence system” as prohibited technology, rather than notifiable technology, for covered national-security transactions involving countries of concern. The proposal’s definition includes generative systems and certain data systems, software, hardware, applications, tools or utilities operating in whole or part using such a system.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The publication does not establish that the proposal will be adopted in this form, how it will be applied in specific transactions, or its realized effects on investment, research or model development.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Treasury estimates annual direct compliance costs of $2.772–$5.86 million and about 20,000 person-hours. It assumes 200 potentially covered transactions per year, doubling a historical-data average to account for undercounting; the notification-cost estimate further assumes all 200 transactions are notifiable. These are ex ante estimates, not observed costs.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Treasury says the existing Outbound Investment Security Program received approximately 100 notifications concerning semiconductor and AI industry investments over about 21 months. This is the prior program’s notification count, not a measured forecast for the proposed rule.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Treasury separately estimates U.S. Government IT development costs of $4–$5 million and additional annual system-maintenance costs of $2–$3 million. It estimates under $1 million in FY2027 personnel costs for compliance promotion, while saying it lacks specific estimates for future outreach and enforcement costs. These are agency estimates, not actual expenditure; they are separate from the $2.772–$5.86 million annual direct compliance-cost estimate.

evidence_gaps.description: The document is a proposed rule. Treasury has not completed the notice-and-comment process, and the final definitions, covered scope and effective date are unknown.
No implementation or observed effect on actual investment, AI research or model development is established by the proposal.

brief.importance_rationale: If adopted, rules that prohibit covered U.S.-person investment in development of defined AI systems in countries of concern could change cross-border capital and development pathways for advanced AI. Importance is 6 because this is a significant proposed rule, but its final scope and practical effect are unresolved.
limitations: This account describes a proposed rule, not enacted law or a final regulatory determination.
The proposed AI definition and transaction coverage may change after public comments.
No actual investment, research or model-development effect is measured.

Treasury’s annual direct-cost estimate ($2.772–$5.86 million; about 20,000 person-hours) is based on assumptions, including 200 potentially covered transactions annually and, for notification costs, that all 200 are notifiable. It is not an observed burden or measure of foregone investment, and Treasury invites comment on its assumptions.

Treasury reports approximately 100 notifications under the existing program over about 21 months, but that historical count concerns semiconductor and AI investments under the earlier regime and is not directly comparable to the proposal’s estimated 200 potentially covered transactions per year across a broader scope.

Treasury separately estimates government IT development ($4–$5 million), annual system maintenance ($2–$3 million) and FY2027 personnel (under $1 million); it gives no specific estimate for future outreach and enforcement. These are not actual expenditures and are separate from the estimated direct compliance costs.

technical.claimed_result: The proposal would prohibit specified covered U.S.-person transactions involving development of defined SI systems for countries of concern; it also sets notification requirements for other specified technologies.
technical.compute_or_cost: Treasury estimates $2.772–$5.86 million in annual direct compliance costs and approximately 20,000 person-hours. The estimate assumes 200 potentially covered transactions annually, double the approximate 100-transaction annual average inferred from PitchBook data for 2023–2025 to account for possible undercounting. The notification-cost estimate assumes all 200 transactions are notifiable; Treasury expects some to prove outside coverage or prohibited and therefore not notifiable. These are regulatory-analysis estimates, not measured costs. Separately, Treasury estimates U.S. Government IT development at $4–$5 million and additional annual maintenance at $2–$3 million, plus under $1 million in FY2027 personnel costs for compliance promotion; specific future outreach and enforcement costs are unavailable. These public-sector estimates are not actual spending and are distinct from the regulated parties’ annual direct-compliance estimate.
technical.demonstrated_result: The Federal Register establishes publication and the content of a proposed rule. No final rule, implementation or realized investment/research effect is established.
technical.mechanism: The proposal would implement Title VIII of the Defense Production Act through definitions of notifiable and prohibited technologies and covered national-security transactions. Its proposed SI-system definition includes generative systems and associated software, hardware, applications, tools or utilities.
technical.regime: U.S. outbound-investment regulation under a proposed Treasury rule, for covered transactions involving foreign persons and countries of concern. The rulemaking is open through Dec 7, 2026.
technical.strongest_baseline: Existing Part 850 outbound-investment regulations; Treasury says the proposal retains much of that framework while implementing Title VIII and placing development of any proposed SI system within prohibited technology. Treasury also reports approximately 100 notifications under the existing program over about 21 months; that historical count is not a directly comparable estimate for the proposed rule’s broader transaction set.

brief.title: U.S. Treasury proposes prohibiting covered outbound investment in development of defined AI systems for countries of concern
brief.why_it_matters: If finalized, this proposal could materially change U.S.-person investment in covered foreign AI development and the compliance boundaries around frontier systems. Treasury estimates $2.772–$5.86 million in annual direct costs and approximately 20,000 person-hours, but these depend on estimated transaction counts and assumptions about notification and diligence; no actual compliance or investment effects are measured. Separately, Treasury estimates $4–$5 million for government IT development and $2–$3 million in annual maintenance, with future enforcement costs not specifically estimated.
